title: Paul’s Greeting and the One Church
english: By the same holy Cyril, Archbishop of Alexandria: a few fragments on the First Epistle to the Corinthians.

“Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 1:1). The inspired Paul says that he has been sent by Christ, by the good pleasure of God the Father. For this, I think, is what “through the will of God” means (1 Corinthians 1:1). Since the Father’s willing and working are through the Son, we say that it is again through the Son that the saints have been appointed to their apostleship.

“And Sosthenes the brother,” and so on (1 Corinthians 1:1). Paul makes it plain that the power of the preaching will benefit not only the Corinthians but also all who have been called in Christ to the sanctification that comes through faith, when he says, “to those sanctified in Christ in every place, theirs and ours” (1 Corinthians 1:2). For the Law did not command this to be done in every place; it commanded them to come to the divine temple itself in Jerusalem (Deuteronomy 12:13–14). It feared, as one would expect, how easily their minds could be carried away: if they were commanded to worship or sacrifice in every place, they might perhaps take the Law as a pretext for turning to more shameful things, and worship carved images, setting up temples and altars for themselves.

But now that we who come from the Gentiles have been called, through faith in Christ, into a close bond with God, and have been enriched with the security that comes through the Holy Spirit, we are commanded to worship, not all of us in Jerusalem, but in every place. This, then, was what was spoken through the prophets: “And they shall worship the Lord, each one from his own place” (Zephaniah 2:11).

So he writes, together with Sosthenes, to the church of God, which Christ presented to himself (Ephesians 5:27). And who were seen to be that church? All who have been sanctified and called through Christ to justification, and who call upon his name “in every place, theirs and ours” (1 Corinthians 1:2), that is, whether in the land of the Jews or in the cities and countries of the Gentiles. He proclaims Christ to be God by nature, and with him and through him he renders glory to God the Father. For he names the sanctified “the church of God,” and yet he assigns them to Christ, saying, “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9).

“Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 1:3). He crowns those who have believed with the grace that comes from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. For through him and in him all things come from God the Father. He is co-giver and co-provider, with the one who begot him, of the good things from above, and he distributes the gifts from heaven. He himself is the peace of all (Ephesians 2:14), and by the grace that comes from himself he makes radiant principalities, thrones and authorities (Colossians 1:16), and, to put it simply, every rational creature.

“But be joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment” (1 Corinthians 1:10). It was both necessary and wise to persuade them that they ought to take their honor from the Master’s name, as the Master himself says through one of the holy prophets: “But those who serve me shall be called by a new name, which shall be blessed upon the earth” (Isaiah 65:15–16). For we have been named Christians, and we are rich in the new name. Some are rightly deprived of it: those who desert the right teaching of the Church and give themselves to deceiving spirits (1 Timothy 4:1) and to the wonder-mongering of certain unholy false teachers. They have taken those teachers’ name, and very fittingly, for they are not Christ’s. They have each taken a share in the blasphemy against him and have been split into differing opinions and judgments, although Christ called his own in peace.

It was needful also to persuade them that Christ himself is one and is not divided (1 Corinthians 1:13). So we are all one in Christ (Galatians 3:28), and for this we have been joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment, since he has bound us into one soul by a spiritual union, he who says of us to God the Father, “I desire that, as I and you are one, so they too in […]” (John 17:21–22).
